extraction.name: XTREME-S
extraction.description: XTREME-S is a benchmark to evaluate universal cross-lingual speech representations in many languages. It covers four task families: speech recognition, classification, speech-to-text translation, and retrieval. The benchmark includes 102 languages from 10+ language families, 3 different domains, and 4 task families, aiming to simplify multilingual speech representation evaluation and catalyze research in 'universal' speech representation learning. Datasets and fine-tuning scripts are made easily accessible through the HuggingFace platform.
extraction.creator: Alexis Conneau, Ankur Bapna, Yu Zhang, Min Ma, Patrick von Platen, Anton Lozhkov, Colin Cherry, Ye Jia, Clara Rivera, Mihir Kale, Daan Van Esch, Vera Axelrod, Simran Khanuja, Jonathan H. Clark, Orhan Firat, Michael Auli, Sebastian Ruder, Jason Riesa, Melvin Johnson
extraction.publisher: Google Research, Hugging Face, Meta AI
extraction.citeAs: Conneau, A., Bapna, A., Zhang, Y., Ma, M., von Platen, P., Lozhkov, A., Cherry, C., Jia, Y., Rivera, C., Kale, M., Van Esch, D., Axelrod, V., Khanuja, S., Clark, J. extraction.rai:dataCollection: XTREME-S builds on existing multilingual speech datasets (FLEURS, MLS, VoxPopuli, CoVoST-2, MINDS-14) and introduces a new dataset (FLEURS) covering 102 languages. Data collection involves sourcing from public corpora (e.g., LibriVox for MLS, European Parliament sessions for VoxPopuli, Wikipedia sentences for speech retrieval tasks) and ensuring diversity in languages, domains, and tasks. The benchmark emphasizes few-shot learning with training sets ranging from a few hours to a few hundred hours of labeled data per language.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Software Collection, Web Scraping
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Data sources include: FLEURS (2009 n-way parallel sentences from FLoRes dev and devtest sets in 102 languages), MLS (Multilingual LibriSpeech derived from LibriVox audiobooks in 8 languages), VoxPopuli (400k hours of unannotated speech and transcriptions/translations in 23 languages), CoVoST-2 (speech translation corpus covering 21 language pairs into English), and MINDS-14 (intent classification task from spoken data in 14 language varieties). Additional sources include Wikipedia sentences for speech retrieval tasks and Common Crawl for text data.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Preprocessing involves creating train-dev-test splits (e.g., 1509/150/350 sentences for FLEURS-ASR), ensuring speaker diversity between train and dev/test sets, and standardizing task metrics (e.g., WER for ASR, BLEU for speech translation, accuracy for classification). For speech retrieval, embeddings are computed for speech and text, and candidates are augmented with 100k Wikipedia sentences per language. Multilingual fine-tuning is encouraged to reduce variance and improve generalization.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotations include speech transcriptions (ASR), translations (speech-to-text translation), language identification labels (FLEURS-LangID), and intent classification labels (MINDS-14). For FLEURS, 2-3 recordings per sentence are collected, and train/dev/test splits are created with distinct speakers. For MINDS-14, monolingual datasets are merged into a multilingual dataset with a 30-20-50% train-dev-test split. Speech retrieval tasks use ranking loss to fine-tune siamese networks for embedding matching.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: HuggingFace platform (https://hf.co/datasets/google/xtreme_sspeech) for dataset access and fine-tuning scripts. Annotation tools are not explicitly mentioned, but the benchmark leverages existing datasets with their original annotations.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: For Fleurs-LangID, speakers are different between train and dev/test sets to avoid overfitting on speaker ID. The benchmark encourages reporting average results over multiple random seeds to minimize variance (e.g., 5 seeds for MINDS-14). Discrepancies in performance across language groups (e.g., Western European vs. Sub-Saharan African) are analyzed and attributed to differences in unlabeled data availability.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 2-3 recordings per sentence for FLEURS-ASR; 1 label per item for MINDS-14 and Fleurs-LangID; variable for speech retrieval tasks (depends on candidate pool size).
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: Datasets and fine-tuning scripts are made publicly available via HuggingFace. The benchmark encourages reproducibility and provides guidelines for submissions. Updates to datasets (e.g., FLEURS) may include minor improvements or replacements of low-quality recordings, with changes documented on the platform. The benchmark is designed to be accessible and encourages community contributions.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The benchmark aims to enable speech technology for under-represented languages, giving speakers of low-resource languages an equal voice on the internet and the ability to share their culture. It addresses the pressing need for multilingual speech understanding systems in a world with ~6,900 languages.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Performance gaps are observed between language groups (e.g., Western European languages perform better than Sub-Saharan African languages), attributed to differences in unlabeled data availability (e.g., MLS and VoxPopuli have more data for Western European languages). The benchmark acknowledges these biases and encourages research to reduce such gaps.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: XTREME-S focuses on linguistic aspects of speech and does not evaluate nonlinguistic/paralinguistic aspects (e.g., speech synthesis or voice conversion). Tasks are limited to read-speech, parliamentary speech, and e-banking domains. The benchmark does not cover all 6,900 languages but includes 102 diverse languages. Some datasets (e.g., FLEURS) may have minor updates in future versions.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, Testing, Validation, and Fine-Tuning for multilingual speech representation learning. The benchmark is designed to evaluate cross-lingual transfer learning, data-efficient speech recognition, and universal speech representation models. It supports research in low-resource language modeling and multilingual speech-to-text translation.
